869.title: Keeping it abroad (Daniel 1)
869.hook: young exiles keep their food laws at the king's court
869.howItsDone: Jews who keep kosher find ways to keep it while traveling, at work and at other people's tables, and the story of Daniel and his friends is told as an example of keeping Jewish practice far from home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esther went in to the king uncalled and named Haman, the enemy, at her own table. Your line was if I perish, I perish. Today, a new book, and another royal court.

A plate arrives from the king's own table. In Babylon, King Nebuchadnezzar has ordered some young captives from Judah trained for his court: good-looking, quick, skilled in learning. They'll learn the tongue of the Chaldeans, eat the king's food and drink his wine. Among them are four young men: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. First, the court renames them. Daniel becomes Belteshazzar. Hananiah becomes Shadrach, Mishael becomes Meshach, Azariah becomes Abed-nego. New names, a new language, new books. They accept all of it. Then the plate comes, and Daniel draws a line.
screen: `CAPTIVES TRAINED FOR THE KING.` → `FOUR NEW NAMES.` → `THEN THE KING'S PLATE.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank." Purposed in his heart: the decision is made inside before it's said out loud. The text doesn't spell out why the king's food would defile him. Some readers point to the food laws of the Torah. Some say the food and wine had been offered to idols. Some hear something simpler: a captive who won't depend on the king's table for everything. What the text does show is how he does it. He doesn't make a scene. He asks the official in charge, who is afraid: if these young men look worse than the others, the king will have his head. So Daniel offers a test. "Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink." Pulse means plain food from seeds: vegetables, beans. Ten days later, the text says, they look healthier than all the young men who ate the king's portion. And God, it adds, gave the four of them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom. So they study Babylon's books, answer to Babylon's names, serve Babylon's king, and still keep one thing that marks who they are. Live fully where you are, and keep something the place can't take away.

segments.voice: Choose one small thing you do that marks who you are, a blessing before you eat, a minute of quiet, a candle, a word of thanks before sleep, and picture the place where it's hardest to keep: a work trip, a loud lunchroom, a hospital, a tired day. See yourself doing it there anyway, quietly, without a speech. If you pray, ask in words from your tradition for help keeping it.
Pulse. The plain food of vegetables and beans Daniel asked for instead of the king's meat and wine. Today's word.
Your line: keep it abroad. The line was drawn in his heart before he ever said a word. Until tomorrow.

870.title: A fourth in the fire (Daniel 3)
870.hook: three young men refuse to bow and walk unharmed in the furnace
870.howItsDone: Jewish teachers tell the story of Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, the Hebrew names of Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego, as an example of refusing to worship an idol even at great risk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Daniel purposed in his heart and asked for pulse and water instead of the king's food. Today, his three friends face something hotter than a menu.

The band is the signal. On the plain of Dura, King Nebuchadnezzar has set up a great image of gold and called every official in the land before it. A herald gives the rule: when you hear the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer and every kind of music, fall down and worship the golden image. Whoever doesn't goes into a burning fiery furnace. The music starts. The whole plain goes down. Three men don't: Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego, the friends from yesterday. Someone reports them, and the king, in a rage, gives them one more chance.
screen: `A GOLDEN IMAGE ON THE PLAIN.` → `THE MUSIC IS THE SIGNAL.` → `THREE MEN DON'T BOW.`

segments.voice: Their answer turns on three small words. In the King James words: "If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up." But if not. They don't bargain. They don't say, we'll stand because we know we'll be rescued. They say God is able, and even if no rescue comes, the answer is still no. The furnace is heated seven times hotter than usual; the men who throw them in are killed by the heat. Then the king jumps up, astonished. He counts. "Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt." Four. The fourth, he says, looks like a son of the gods. Later the king himself says their God sent his angel. They went in bound. Now they walk loose. When they come out, the text lists what isn't there: not a hair singed, their coats unchanged, not even the smell of fire on them. The story doesn't say the fire wasn't real. It says they weren't alone in it.

Say what you hope will come of it, then the other half, but if not, and ask whether you'd still do it with the happy ending taken away. If you pray, ask in words from your tradition not to be alone in it.
If not. The three words the friends anchor their answer on: God is able, but if not, the answer is still no. Today's word.
Your line: not alone in the fire. God is able, but if not, the answer is still no. That's day eight hundred seventy.

871.title: Weighed in the balances (Daniel 5)
871.hook: the writing on the wall: weighed, and found wanting
871.howItsDone: Some Jews keep a practice called cheshbon ha-nefesh, an accounting of the soul, looking honestly at their day or their year, especially in the month of Elul before Rosh Hashanah, and some do it each night before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three men said but if not, walked loose in the furnace, and the king counted four. Your line was not alone in the fire. Today, a different king, and a different kind of fire.

King Belshazzar has been tasting wine at his great feast when he calls for the cups: the gold and silver vessels taken out of the Temple in Jerusalem. He and his lords, his wives and concubines drink from them, and praise gods of gold and silver, brass, iron, wood and stone. In the same hour, the fingers of a man's hand appear and write on the plaster of the palace wall, near the lampstand. The king watches the hand write. His face changes. In the King James words, "his knees smote one against another." Nobody in the room can read it.
screen: `HOLY CUPS AT A ROYAL PARTY.` → `A HAND WRITES ON THE WALL.` → `NOBODY CAN READ IT.`

segments.voice: The king's wise men fail. The queen remembers a man from the old king's days, Daniel, and he's brought in. Belshazzar offers him scarlet clothes, a gold chain, a high place in the kingdom. Daniel's first words: "Let thy gifts be to thyself." He'll read it, but not for pay. Then, before reading, he tells the king a story the king already knows: how his father Nebuchadnezzar grew proud and was brought low. And then: "thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this." Though you knew. The charge isn't ignorance. It's knowing better and lifting the holy cups anyway. Then Daniel reads the wall. "MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN." Mene: God has numbered your kingdom and finished it. Then: "TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting." Peres: your kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians. Weighed. Not shouted at, not argued with: put on a scale, and the scale reads light. The text doesn't linger. "In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain." It's a frightening chapter, and it leaves a plain question for an ordinary evening: if today were set on a scale, what would be in the pans?

segments.voice: Picture an old balance scale and go back over today so far, or yesterday if it's early: in one pan, what you did well, a kindness, a job done right; in the other, what was wanting, a sharp word, a time you knew better. Don't argue with the scale or punish yourself with it; just look, and choose one good thing to add to the first pan before tonight. If you pray, bring both pans before God in words from your tradition.
Tekel. The word on the wall that Daniel reads as weighed, and found wanting. Today's word.
Your line: weighed in the balance. The charge wasn't ignorance; it was knowing better. Day eight hundred seventy-one, done.

872.title: Windows toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6)
872.hook: Daniel keeps praying three times a day, windows open toward Jerusalem, lions or not
872.tomorrow: They that be wise shall shine (Daniel 12:3)
872.howItsDone: Jewish tradition sets three services a day, Shacharit in the morning, Minchah in the afternoon and Maariv in the evening, facing toward Jerusalem, and the Talmud (Berakhot 31a) learns from Daniel 6 that one should pray in a room with windows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tekel: a hand wrote on a palace wall, and Daniel read it as weighed, and found wanting. Today, the same man, a new king, and a trap.

The trap is a law. Under a new king, Darius, Daniel rises so high that the other officials go looking for something to accuse him of, and find nothing. In the King James words: "We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God." So they bring the king a flattering idea. For thirty days, let no one ask a petition of any god or man except the king. Whoever does goes into the den of lions. The king signs it, under the law of the Medes and Persians, which can't be changed. Everyone knows what Daniel does every day.
screen: `NO FAULT BUT HIS FAITH.` → `A LAW FOR THIRTY DAYS.` → `SIGNED, AND IT CAN'T CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Here is what he does: "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." Look at what he doesn't do. He doesn't close the windows. He doesn't switch to praying in secret for a month. He doesn't march into the square to make a point either. He goes home, to his own room, and does what he did yesterday. The courage in this story looks like a habit. And notice which way the windows face: toward Jerusalem, a city far away. He can't see it. He faces it anyway. The officials catch him. The king, who doesn't want this, tries until sundown to save him and can't, and Daniel goes into the den. At dawn the king runs to the stone and calls. Daniel answers: "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me." This chapter left marks on Jewish prayer. Jewish tradition sets prayer for morning, afternoon and evening, said facing toward Jerusalem, and the Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, learns from this very verse that a person should pray in a room with windows.

segments.voice: If there's a window near you, turn toward it or open it a little; if not, turn toward the light in the room, and let it stand for whatever you face each day: a place, a hope, a person, God. If you pray, this is your time, in words from your tradition or in silence, the way Daniel prayed in his own room; if you don't, simply sit facing out and let the day come in.
Jerusalem. The city Daniel's open windows faced, three times a day, lions or not, as he did aforetime. Today's word.
Your line: as he did aforetime. In this story, courage looks like a habit. See you tomorrow.

873.title: They that be wise shall shine (Daniel 12:3)
873.hook: the wise "shall shine as the brightness of the firmament"
873.howItsDone: In chavruta, a traditional way of Jewish study in pairs, two partners read a text aloud and explain it to each other, so that teaching is part of learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Daniel prayed with his windows open toward Jerusalem, as he did aforetime. Today, the last chapter of Daniel.

What does a book of furnaces and lions end on? Not on a court story. The later chapters of Daniel turn into visions: beasts rising from the sea, kings rising and falling, messengers who explain and still leave much unexplained. By the last chapter the vision has reached its darkest point. In the King James words, "there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time." And right there, in the trouble, the text stops to say who will be shining.
screen: `FROM COURT STORIES TO VISIONS.` → `A TIME OF TROUBLE.` → `THEN, WHO WILL SHINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the line: "And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever." Two kinds of light. The firmament is the whole sky, the bright dome over everything. The stars are points of light, each on its own in the dark. Who are the wise? The Hebrew word is maskilim. A chapter earlier, the same book describes them: "they that understand among the people shall instruct many." So in Daniel, the wise aren't the ones who keep wisdom to themselves. They pass it on, and those who turn many to righteousness shine like stars. Some readers hear in maskilim both at once: those who are wise, and those who make others wise. Then a surprise near the very end. Daniel himself, who read the wall and the dreams of kings, says of his own vision: "I heard, but I understood not." He asks how it will end, and is told: "Go thy way, Daniel: for the words are closed up and sealed till the time of the end." The man who read the wall doesn't get every answer, and he's still told to go his way. You don't need to understand everything to teach the one thing you do. A star doesn't light the whole sky. It shines where it is.

segments.voice: Look over what you've learned on this path lately, a word, a story, a line, and pick one thing you understand well enough to say in a sentence or two. Think of one person who might like to hear it, and say the sentence to yourself, plainly, the way you'd say it to them; one star's worth is enough.
Maskilim. The wise in Daniel's last chapter: those who instruct many, who shine like the sky and the stars. Today's word.

874.title: The return (Ezra 1)
874.hook: Cyrus of Persia lets the exiles go home to rebuild
874.carry: the ones who go and the ones who send
874.howItsDone: Moving to the land of Israel is called aliyah, going up, the same picture of going up that Cyrus's decree uses, and Jews who move to Israel today are said to make aliyah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the maskilim, the wise who instruct many, shine as the firmament, and those who turn many to righteousness, as the stars. Today, a new book, and a door opens.

"Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia." A proclamation goes out through a whole empire, spoken aloud and put in writing. The God of heaven, says the king, has given him all the kingdoms of the earth, and charged him to build a house in Jerusalem, in Judah. Then the line that opens the way home. In the King James words: "Who is there among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem." After all the chapters of loss, the book of Ezra opens with a door.
screen: `A PROCLAMATION FROM CYRUS.` → `BUILD A HOUSE IN JERUSALEM.` → `LET HIM GO UP.`

segments.voice: The book opens by saying why: it was "in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled," and "the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus." A foreign king, and the text sees God moving through him anyway. Help, again, from an unexpected place. Now listen to the shape of the decree. It isn't an order. It's an invitation: let him go up. Not everyone does. The ones who rose up to go, the text says, were all those whose spirit God had stirred. Others stay, and the text doesn't scold them. The people around them help instead, strengthening the travelers with silver and gold, goods and animals, and freewill offerings for the house of God. A return needs both: the ones who go and the ones who send. Then Cyrus does one more thing. He brings out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from Jerusalem, counts them out to a leader of Judah, and sends them home. A few days ago, in Daniel, a king drank wine from vessels like these. Now they're packed for the road. The return doesn't begin with a wall or a Temple. It begins with going up, and carrying back what was taken.
screen: `GOD STIRRED UP A FOREIGN KING.` · `LET HIM GO UP: AN INVITATION.` · `THOSE AROUND THEM SENT GIFTS.` · then, large: `THE VESSELS GO HOME.` · then: `GOING UP, CARRYING BACK.`

segments.voice: Think of something of yours that got left somewhere along the way: a song your family sang, a recipe nobody makes anymore, a language you grew up hearing, a skill you set down. Don't scold yourself for the distance, the decree didn't; just hold it the way an exile might hold the name of a city, and find the first small step that would carry it back. 875.title: Weeping and shouting (Ezra 3:10–13)
875.hook: at the new foundation the old weep and others shout, and no one can tell the sounds apart
875.howItsDone: At a Jewish wedding, by tradition, a glass is broken at the end of the ceremony, which some explain as remembering the destruction of Jerusalem even at a moment of great joy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the return: Cyrus said let him go up, and it took the ones who go and the ones who send. Today, they lay a foundation, and the week ends.

Two sounds rise from the same building site, and both are loud. The builders have just laid the foundation of the new house of the LORD in Jerusalem. The priests stand in their robes with trumpets. The Levites, sons of Asaph, stand with cymbals. They sing back and forth, praising and giving thanks, in the King James words, "because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel." The people answer with a great shout. It should be a simple, happy scene. It isn't simple.
screen: `THE FOUNDATION IS LAID.` → `TRUMPETS, CYMBALS, A SONG.` → `A GREAT SHOUT.`

segments.voice: Here's what the text says next: "But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy." The old men had seen the first Temple. Standing at the beginning of the second, they weep. The text doesn't say why. Maybe grief for what was lost. Maybe the memory of what used to stand there. Maybe relief, after so long. Maybe all of it at once. And many others shout for joy at a beginning. Notice who is weeping: not doubters on the edge of the crowd, but priests and Levites, the same groups the text set at the center of the song, along with the heads of families. Then: "So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people." The text refuses to separate them. It doesn't say the joy drowned out the tears, or that the old men should have cheered up. Both sounds rise together, and the noise, it says, was heard afar off. Anyone listening from a distance heard one sound, made of both.
screen: `THE OLD MEN WEEP.` · `OTHERS SHOUT FOR JOY.` · `NO ONE CAN TELL THE SOUNDS APART.` · then, large: `THE NOISE WAS HEARD AFAR OFF.` · then: `ONE SOUND, MADE OF BOTH.`
